lessons.title: 1. What is Django?
lessons.html:
• Django = a Python web framework that lets you build web apps quickly with minimal code. Created 2003–2005.
  • It handles the boring parts: routing, database access, forms, admin panel — so you focus on your app logic.
  • Django is a back-end framework. It runs on the server, talks to the database, and sends HTML back to the browser.
  • Key idea: Django uses the MVT pattern — Model, View, Template — which is Django's version of MVC.

lessons.title: 2. MVT Architecture
lessons.html:
• Model = Python class mapped to a database table. Handles all data storage and retrieval (ORM).
  • View = Python function (or class) that receives an HTTP request, does logic, and returns an HTTP response. This is what MVC calls a Controller.
  • Template = HTML file with special Django tags. Generates the page the user sees. This is what MVC calls a View.
  • urls.py = the router — maps a URL to the right view.
  • Flow: Browser → urls.py → views.py → (optionally) Model + Template → HTTP response back to browser.
  • Trap: Django's "View" ≠ MVC's "View". In Django, the View is the logic layer (MVC Controller). The Template is the presentation layer (MVC View).

lessons.title: 3. Virtual Environment
lessons.html:
• Always work inside a virtual environment — an isolated Python installation just for your project. Avoids dependency conflicts between projects.
  • Create + activate:
    # create
python -m venv my_env
# activate (Linux/Mac)
source my_env/bin/activate
# activate (Windows)
my_env\Scripts\activate
  • Install Django:
    (my_env) $ python -m pip install django
  • Save dependencies:
    (my_env) $ pip freeze > requirements.txt
  • Trap: Never pip install without activating the venv first — you'll pollute the global Python.

lessons.title: 4. Create a Project
lessons.html:
• Create project:
    (my_env) $ django-admin startproject django_project .
    The . puts the files in the current folder instead of a nested folder.
  • Project anatomy:
    • manage.py — your command tool (runserver, migrate, startapp…)
    • settings.py — all configuration (INSTALLED_APPS, DATABASES, TEMPLATES…)
    • urls.py — the main URL router
    • wsgi.py — interface for traditional servers (Gunicorn, Apache)
    • asgi.py — interface for async servers (Channels, Daphne)
    • __init__.py — marks the folder as a Python package
  • Run the server:
    (my_env) $ python manage.py runserver
    Then open http://127.0.0.1:8000

lessons.title: 5. Create an App
lessons.html:
• A project = the whole website. An app = one feature/module inside the project. One project can have many apps (e.g. pages, meetings, blog).
  • Create app:
    (my_env) $ python manage.py startapp pages
  • Register it in settings.py:
    INSTALLED_APPS = [
    ...
    'pages',  # add your app here
]
  • Trap: If you forget to add the app to INSTALLED_APPS, Django ignores it — models won't migrate, templates won't be found in some configs.

lessons.title: 6. First View
lessons.html:
• A view is a Python function that takes a request and returns a response.
  • The simplest response is HttpResponse:
    • from django.shortcuts import render
from django.http import HttpResponse

def home_page_view(request):
    return HttpResponse("Hello word")
  • The request object contains everything about the incoming HTTP request: method (GET/POST), user, headers, POST data.
  • Trap: Every view must return a response. Forgetting the return crashes with a ValueError.

lessons.title: 7. URL Routing
lessons.html:
• Django routes URLs in two steps: project urls.py → app urls.py.
  • App urls.py (create this file manually in your app folder):
    from django.urls import path
from .views import home_page_view

urlpatterns = [
    path('home/', home_page_view, name='home'),
]
  • Project urls.py — include the app's URLs:
    from django.contrib import admin
from django.urls import path, include

urlpatterns = [
    path('admin/', admin.site.urls),
    path('pages/', include('pages.urls')),
]
  • Now visiting /pages/home/ calls home_page_view.
  • name= gives the URL a name so you can reverse it in templates: {% url 'home' %} instead of hardcoding /pages/home/.
  • Trap: include() takes a string 'pages.urls', not pages.urls.

lessons.title: 1. Multi-App Project Structure
lessons.html:
• The Meeting Planner project has two apps: website (home + about pages) and meetings (the meeting data).
  • Structure:
    meetings_planner/
  meetings/          ← app: meetings logic
  meetings_planner/  ← project config folder
  website/           ← app: public pages
  manage.py
  • Each app gets registered in INSTALLED_APPS:
    INSTALLED_APPS = [
    ...
    'website',
    'meetings',
]
  • Each app has its own urls.py. The project's urls.py includes both.

lessons.title: 2. render() and Templates
lessons.html:
• Instead of returning raw text with HttpResponse, real views use render() to send an HTML template.
    • from django.shortcuts import render

def home_view(request):
    return render(request, 'website/home.html')
  • render(request, template_name, context) — the third argument is a context dict: data you want to use in the template.
    • def home_view(request):
    context = {'meetings': Meeting.objects.all()}
    return render(request, 'website/home.html', context=context)
  • Template location: put HTML files at appname/templates/appname/filename.html. The double appname/ avoids name clashes between apps.
  • Trap: If you put templates directly in appname/templates/ without the sub-folder, two apps both having home.html will clash — Django picks one unpredictably.

lessons.title: 3. URL Parameters
lessons.html:
• To capture a value from the URL (like a meeting ID), use angle brackets in the path:
    • path('meetings/<int:id>/', views.detail, name='detail')
  • Django passes id as a keyword argument to the view:
    • def detail(request, id):
    meeting = Meeting.objects.get(pk=id)
    return render(request, 'meetings/detail.html', {'meeting': meeting})
  • Type converters: <int:id> matches integers only. Others: <str:slug>, <slug:slug>, <uuid:id>.
  • Trap: Using Meeting.objects.get(pk=id) raises Meeting.DoesNotExist if the ID doesn't exist — your app crashes. Use get_object_or_404 instead (see next lesson).

lessons.title: 4. get_object_or_404
lessons.html:
• get_object_or_404 is the safe way to look up an object by ID. If nothing is found, it returns a proper 404 page instead of crashing.
    • from django.shortcuts import get_object_or_404, render
from .models import Meeting

def detail(request, id):
    meeting = get_object_or_404(Meeting, id=id)
    return render(request, 'meetings/detail.html', {'meeting': meeting})
  • Import it from django.shortcuts (same place as render).
  • Rule of thumb: Always use get_object_or_404 in views when looking up by user-supplied ID. Use .get() only in internal scripts where you're sure the object exists.

lessons.title: 5. Template Language Basics
lessons.html:
• Django templates are HTML files with extra syntax:
  • Display a variable: {{ variable }}
  • Tags (logic): {% tag %}
  • Filters: {{ variable|filtername }}
  • For loop:
    <ul>
{% for meeting in meetings %}
  <li>{{ meeting.title }}</li>
{% endfor %}
</ul>
  • If/else:
    {% if meetings %}
  <p>{{ meetings|length }} meetings</p>
{% else %}
  <p>No meetings yet.</p>
{% endif %}
  • Comments: {# this is a comment #} or {% comment %}...{% endcomment %}
  • Link to a named URL: <a href="{% url 'detail' meeting.id %}">
  • Trap: Django template syntax uses {% %} not <% %> (that's other frameworks). And {{ }} for output, not <%= %>.

lessons.title: 6. Template Inheritance
lessons.html:
• Inheritance lets you define a base template with the common layout (navbar, footer, CSS) and child templates that just fill in the unique content. No copy-pasting HTML.
  • base.html:
    <!DOCTYPE html>
<html lang="en">
<head>
  <meta charset="UTF-8">
  <title>{% block title %}{% endblock %}</title>
</head>
<body>
  {% block content %}
  {% endblock %}
</body>
</html>
  • about.html (child):
    {% extends "base.html" %}
{% block title %}About{% endblock %}
{% block content %}
  <h2>Meeting Planner — Tek-up</h2>
{% endblock %}
  • Traps: {% extends %} must be the very first line of the child template. Any HTML before it is silently ignored. Block names must match exactly.
  • {% include %} is different — it inserts a template fragment (like a navbar snippet) without inheritance. Use {% include 'navbar.html' %}.

lessons.title: 7. Static Files
lessons.html:
• Static files = CSS, JavaScript, images. Django serves them from each app's static/ folder during development.
  • In settings.py: STATIC_URL = 'static/' (already there by default).
  • In your template, load the tag first, then use it:
    {% load static %}
<!DOCTYPE html>
<html>
<head>
  <link rel="stylesheet"
        href="{% static 'website/style.css' %}">
</head>
  • File lives at: website/static/website/style.css
  • Trap: Forgetting {% load static %} at the top of the template causes a TemplateSyntaxError: Invalid block tag 'static'.
  • STATIC_ROOT = where collectstatic gathers all static files for production deployment. Not needed during development.

cards.q: What does MVT stand for in Django, and what does each letter do?
cards.ans: Model (database layer, ORM), View (business logic, processes request), Template (HTML presentation layer). urls.py connects URLs to views.
cards.why: Django's MVT maps to MVC: Model=Model, View=Controller, Template=View.

cards.q: How is Django's MVT different from the classic MVC pattern?
cards.ans: In MVC: Model=data, View=presentation, Controller=logic. In Django MVT: Model=data, Template=presentation (MVC View), View=logic (MVC Controller). The naming is swapped for View/Template vs View/Controller.
cards.why: This is a classic Part 2 written question in Tek-up exams.

cards.q: What is the purpose of a virtual environment in Django development?
cards.ans: It creates an isolated Python environment per project so each project can have its own dependency versions without conflicts. E.g. app1 uses Django 4.2, app2 uses Django 5.1 — no clash.
cards.why: Appear in Part 2 as 'explain with example'.

cards.q: What command creates a new Django project named 'mysite'?
cards.ans:
django-admin startproject mysite .
The dot (.) puts files in the current folder. Without it, Django creates a nested mysite/mysite/ structure.

cards.q: Name the files inside a Django project folder and their role.
cards.ans: manage.py = command runner (runserver, migrate, startapp). settings.py = all config. urls.py = main URL router. wsgi.py = WSGI server interface. asgi.py = async server interface. __init__.py = marks it as a package.
cards.why: Exam Q3 tested which files are used for deployment (asgi.py, wsgi.py).

cards.q: What command creates a new app named 'pages' inside a Django project?
cards.why: Exam Q4 tested the exact syntax — answer C is correct.

cards.q: After creating an app, what must you do in settings.py?
cards.ans:
Add the app name to INSTALLED_APPS. Example:
INSTALLED_APPS = [
    ...
    'pages',  # your new app
]
cards.why: Without this, Django ignores the app. Models won't migrate.

cards.q: What does this view return?
cards.out: An HTTP 200 response with body: Hello word
cards.why: HttpResponse directly returns text/HTML without a template. Verified running Django 5.1.

cards.q: What crash happens if a view function has no return statement?
cards.code:
def broken_view(request):
    x = 1 + 1  # forgot to return
cards.out: ValueError: The view returned None instead of an HttpResponse object.
cards.why: Django checks the return value and raises ValueError if it's None.

cards.q: Show the two-step URL routing pattern: app urls.py + project urls.py.
cards.ans:
App (pages/urls.py):
from django.urls import path
from .views import home_page_view
urlpatterns = [path('home/', home_page_view, name='home')]

Project (urls.py):
from django.urls import path, include
urlpatterns = [
    path('admin/', admin.site.urls),
    path('pages/', include('pages.urls')),
]
cards.why: include() delegates all /pages/... URLs to the app's own urlpatterns.

cards.q: What does the name= parameter in path() do?
cards.ans: It gives the URL a name so you can reference it by name instead of hardcoding the path. In templates: {% url 'home' %}. In Python: reverse('home'). If the URL path changes later, only the path() call changes — not every template.
cards.why: Classic Part 2 question: 'Role of the name parameter in routes'.

cards.q: What is the trap with include() — which of these is WRONG?
cards.code:
# A:
path('pages/', include(pages.urls))
# B:
path('pages/', include('pages.urls'))
cards.out: A is wrong. include() takes a string 'pages.urls', not the module object pages.urls.
cards.why: Common student mistake: forgetting the quotes around the dotted path.

cards.q: What is the difference between HttpResponse and render()?
cards.ans:
HttpResponse returns raw content (text, HTML string) directly. render() loads a template file, fills it with context data, and returns an HttpResponse — specifically designed for HTML pages. Example: HttpResponse('

Hello

') vs render(request, 'home.html', {'name': 'Malak'})
cards.why: Exam correction Part 2 explicitly asks this question.

cards.q: Why do we put templates in appname/templates/appname/ (double folder)?
cards.ans: To avoid name clashes. If two apps both have templates/home.html, Django picks one unpredictably. With the double folder, one is website/home.html and the other is meetings/home.html — no clash. Always reference templates with the prefix: render(request, 'website/home.html').
cards.why: A subtle trap that causes bugs in multi-app projects.

cards.q: What does get_object_or_404 do that plain .get() doesn't?
cards.ans: If the object doesn't exist, .get() raises ObjectDoesNotExist and Django shows a 500 error (server crash). get_object_or_404 raises Http404 instead, which shows a proper 404 page — better UX and security (don't expose stack traces to users).

cards.q: Complete this URL pattern to capture an integer id from the URL /meetings/5/
cards.why: <int:id> tells Django: match only integers here, and pass the value to the view as a keyword argument named 'id'.

cards.q: Write the template loop that shows a list of meeting titles as links.
cards.ans:
{% for meeting in meetings %}
  • {{ meeting.title }}
    • {% endfor %}
cards.why: {% url 'detail' meeting.id %} generates /meetings/5/ from the named URL. {{ meeting.title }} displays the field.

cards.q: Show base.html and a child template that extends it.
cards.why: extends must be the very first line. Block names must match exactly between parent and child.

cards.q: What is the trap with {% extends %} in a child template?
cards.ans: {% extends 'base.html' %} MUST be the very first line of the template. Any HTML written before it is silently discarded by Django.
cards.why: Classic beginner mistake: putting a DOCTYPE or comment before extends.

cards.q: What error happens when you use {% static %} without {% load static %}?
cards.out: TemplateSyntaxError: Invalid block tag on line 1: 'static'
cards.why: {% load static %} must appear at the top of any template that uses the {% static %} tag.

cards.q: What is the difference between {% include %} and {% extends %}?
cards.ans:
{% extends 'base.html' %} = inheritance: the child template fills blocks inside the parent layout. Only one base allowed per template.
{% include 'navbar.html' %} = composition: inserts a fragment inline. No block system. Can use multiple includes in one template.

cards.q: Name three important settings in settings.py and explain their role.
cards.ans:
1. INSTALLED_APPS — list of activated apps (built-in + yours). Without it, Django ignores your app.
2. DATABASES — database connection config (engine, name, host, user, password).
3. STATIC_URL — URL prefix for static files. STATIC_ROOT — where collectstatic gathers files for production.
Bonus: TEMPLATES — list of template engines and their settings (DIRS, APP_DIRS).
cards.why: Exam Part 2 Q2 asks exactly this.

cards.q: [Part 3 — Ex1] Complete the project urls.py so that /pages/home/ works.
cards.code:
# django_project/urls.py
from django.contrib import admin
from django.urls import path, _____(1)_____

urlpatterns = [
    path('admin/', admin.site.urls),
    path('pages/', _____(2)_____('pages.urls')),
]
cards.out:
(1) include
(2) include

Full solution:
from django.contrib import admin
from django.urls import path, include

urlpatterns = [
    path('admin/', admin.site.urls),
    path('pages/', include('pages.urls')),
]

Verified: reverse('home') -> /pages/home/ OK
cards.why: (1) import include from django.urls. (2) include() delegates all /pages/... URLs to pages/urls.py. The argument is a string — forgetting quotes causes NameError.

cards.q: [Part 3 — Ex2] Complete the app-level urls.py for the 'pages' app.
cards.code:
# pages/urls.py
from django.urls import _____(1)_____
from _____(2)_____ import home_page_view

urlpatterns = [
    _____(3)_____('home/', home_page_view, name='home'),
]
cards.out:
(1) path
(2) .views  (dot = this app's views.py)
(3) path

Full solution:
from django.urls import path
from .views import home_page_view

urlpatterns = [
    path('home/', home_page_view, name='home'),
]

Verified: reverse('home') = /pages/home/ OK
cards.why: The .views relative import means 'views.py inside this same app folder'. Using 'views' without a dot fails unless the app is explicitly on the Python path.

cards.q: [Part 3 — Ex3] Complete the views.py for the Meeting Planner home page.
cards.out:
(1) render
(2) 'meetings'
(3) all
(4) context

Full solution:
from django.shortcuts import render
from meetings.models import Meeting

def home_view(request):
    context = {'meetings': Meeting.objects.all()}
    return render(request, 'website/home.html', context=context)

Verified: template for loop renders all meetings OK
cards.why: render() takes: request, template name (prefixed with app name), and a context dict. The key name 'meetings' is what the template uses with {% for meeting in meetings %}.

cards.q: [Part 3 — Ex4] Complete the detail view that safely fetches a Meeting by URL id.
cards.out:
(1) get_object_or_404
(2) id
(3) id  (or pk)

Full solution:
from django.shortcuts import get_object_or_404, render
from .models import Meeting

def detail(request, id):
    meeting = get_object_or_404(Meeting, id=id)
    return render(request, 'meetings/detail.html', {'meeting': meeting})

Verified: found Meeting pk=1 OK; Http404 raised for pk=99999 OK
cards.why: get_object_or_404 catches DoesNotExist and returns a 404 response. Plain .get() causes a 500 server error if the meeting doesn't exist — always use get_object_or_404 in views.

cards.q: [Part 3 — Ex5] Complete the template to list meetings with a fallback for empty list.
cards.code:
{% extends "base.html" %} {% block content %}

Meetings

    _____(1)_____ meeting in meetings _____
  • {{ meeting._____(3)_____ }}
    • _____(4)_____
  • No meetings yet.
    • _____(5)_____
{% endblock %}
cards.why: {% for %}...{% empty %}...{% endfor %} is the standard Django idiom for 'list or fallback'. {% empty %} runs when the iterable has zero items. This pattern appears on every real exam.

cards.q: [Part 3 — Ex6] Complete base.html to load a CSS static file.
cards.code:
_____(1)_____
<!DOCTYPE html>
<html lang="en">
<head>
  <title>{% block title %}{% endblock %}</title>
  <link rel="stylesheet"
        href="{% _____(2)_____ 'website/style.css' %}">
</head>
<body>
  {% block content %}{% endblock %}
</body>
</html>
cards.out:
(1) {% load static %}
(2) static

Full solution:
{% load static %}
<!DOCTYPE html>
<html lang="en">
<head>
  <title>{% block title %}{% endblock %}</title>
  <link rel="stylesheet" href="{% static 'website/style.css' %}">
</head>
<body>
  {% block content %}{% endblock %}
</body>
</html>

File lives at: website/static/website/style.css
Verified: {% load static %} tag available OK
cards.why: {% load static %} must appear before any {% static %} use. Without it: TemplateSyntaxError: Invalid block tag 'static'. STATIC_URL in settings.py controls the URL prefix.

mcq.q: Which command correctly creates a Django application named 'blog'?
mcq.why: python manage.py startapp blog is correct. django-admin is for projects (startproject), not apps. newapp and createapp do not exist — they are made-up commands. This was question 4 on the actual exam.

mcq.q: In Django's MVT pattern, which component handles the business logic and processes HTTP requests?
mcq.why: The View in Django = the Controller in MVC. It receives the HTTP request, runs logic (queries, calculations), and returns a response. The Template handles presentation. The Model handles data. 'Controller' is the MVC name — Django doesn't use that term.

mcq.q: In Django, what is the Template equivalent in classic MVC architecture?
mcq.why: Django Template = MVC View (presentation layer). Django View = MVC Controller (logic layer). The names are swapped — the most common confusion in exams.

mcq.q: Which files are used by default for server deployment in Django? (Choose 2)
mcq.why: wsgi.py = WSGI server interface (Gunicorn, uWSGI, Apache). asgi.py = ASGI server interface (Daphne, Uvicorn — for async/WebSocket). manage.py is for local dev commands. This was exam Q3.

mcq.q: How do you correctly include an app's URLs in the project's urls.py?
mcq.code:
# Which is correct?
# A:
path('blog/', include('blog.urls'))
# B:
path('blog/', include(blog.urls))
# C:
path('blog/urls', blog)
# D:
path('route', my_view)
mcq.why: include() takes a string: 'blog.urls'. Passing the module object blog.urls without quotes raises a NameError (unless you imported it). This was exam Q10.

mcq.q: A URL pattern path('articles/<int:id>/', views.detail) is defined. Which URL will it match?
mcq.why: <int:id> matches only positive integers. hello is a string → no match. Missing the number → no match. 3.5 is a float, not an integer → no match.

mcq.q: What is wrong with this view?
mcq.ok: It returns None — Django will raise ValueError
bad: x = 2 + 2 is a syntax error in Django
mcq.why: Every Django view must return an HttpResponse (or subclass). This function returns None implicitly. Django checks the return value and raises ValueError: The view returned None instead of an HttpResponse object.

mcq.ok: An HttpResponse containing the rendered HTML of home.html with name='Malak' substituted
bad: A string containing the HTML source
A dict with the context data
mcq.why: render() is a shortcut that loads the template, substitutes the context variables, and returns a full HttpResponse object (status 200, Content-Type text/html). It is not a string or a dict.

mcq.q: You create a new app 'shop' but its models are never found by migrate. What is the most likely cause?
mcq.ok: 'shop' is not in INSTALLED_APPS in settings.py
bad: You need to run startapp again
Django only supports one app per project
mcq.why: Django only processes apps that are listed in INSTALLED_APPS. If 'shop' is not there, Django ignores its models.py entirely — no migration files will be created.

mcq.q: What is the correct syntax to display a template variable in Django?
mcq.why: Django uses {{ variable }} for output and {% tag %} for logic. <%= %> is ERB (Ruby). <% %> is ASP/JSP. This was in the exam correction.

mcq.q: What is the correct way to comment a block in a Django template?
bad: {# single line only works for blocks #}
mcq.why: {% comment %}...{% endcomment %} for multi-line blocks. {# ... #} for single-line comments. HTML comments <!-- --> are NOT Django comments — the template engine still evaluates them. This was exam Q12.

mcq.q: What can a Django template NOT do?
mcq.why: Templates handle presentation only. Database access happens in the View (which queries the Model and passes results as context). Templates cannot import Python modules or run ORM queries. This was exam Q7.

mcq.q: Given this urls.py, what URL resolves for {% url 'home' %}?
mcq.code:
urlpatterns = [
    path('pages/', include('pages.urls')),
]
# pages/urls.py:
urlpatterns = [
    path('', views.home_view, name='home'),
]
mcq.why: The project routes /pages/ to the pages app. Inside the app, path('') matches the root of that prefix — so the full URL is /pages/. name='home' resolves to that combined path.

mcq.q: What is the difference between these two views?
mcq.ok: View A returns a plain string; View B loads and renders an HTML template file
bad: View A is for GET, View B is for POST
View B returns JSON, View A returns HTML
mcq.why: HttpResponse takes content directly (string, bytes). render() loads a template file from disk, substitutes context variables, and returns an HttpResponse. For real pages you almost always use render().

mcq.q: What does get_object_or_404(Meeting, pk=5) do if no Meeting with pk=5 exists?
mcq.ok: Raises Http404, Django returns a 404 page
bad: Raises Meeting.DoesNotExist and shows a 500 error
Creates a new Meeting with pk=5
mcq.why: get_object_or_404 catches DoesNotExist and re-raises it as Http404 — resulting in a proper 404 response. Plain .get() raises DoesNotExist which Django turns into a 500 server error (ugly and insecure).

mcq.q: What is the trap in this child template?
mcq.ok: {% extends %} must be the FIRST line — the DOCTYPE before it is silently ignored
bad: DOCTYPE is not allowed in Django templates
{% block content %} needs an id attribute
mcq.why: Django requires {% extends %} to be the very first token in the template. Anything before it (even whitespace or DOCTYPE) is silently discarded. The whole page will render without the DOCTYPE.

topics.dj.orm: ORM queries — filter, get, create, delete
topics.dj.auth: Authentication — User model, login, signup, permissions

steps.say: Every Django app follows the same pattern: a browser sends a request, Django routes it, a view processes it, and a response comes back. Let's trace exactly what happens.
The View is the brain. It may query the database through the Model, fill a Template with the results, and return everything as an HTTP response.
add:
Django's 'View' = MVC's Controller
Django's 'Template' = MVC's View

steps.say: Here is what a view actually looks like in code — the simplest possible one using HttpResponse.
add: Simplest view — from the professor's slides
The {r:request} object arrives → view runs → {g:HttpResponse} goes back to browser

steps.say: And here is how you plug that view into the URL system. Two files work together: the app's urls.py and the project's urls.py.
add:
# pages/urls.py  (app level)
from django.urls import path
from .views import home_page_view

urlpatterns = [
    path('home/', home_page_view, name='home'),
]

# django_project/urls.py  (project level)
from django.urls import path, include

urlpatterns = [
    path('admin/', admin.site.urls),
    path('pages/', include('pages.urls')),
]

URL = /pages/home/
Project sees 'pages/' → hands off to pages.urls
App sees 'home/' → calls home_page_view

steps.say: One last piece: registering the app. Without this line in settings.py, Django ignores your app completely.

add.q: You visit /pages/home/ and get a 404. The view exists and urls.py looks correct. What's the most likely cause?
add.ok: The app is not in INSTALLED_APPS
add.why: Without the app in INSTALLED_APPS, Django never loads its URLs or models. This is the #1 beginner mistake.

steps.say: Let's create a project from scratch and understand every file Django generates.
add:
# 1. Create and activate virtual env
python -m venv my_env
source my_env/bin/activate    # Linux/Mac
# my_env\Scripts\activate    # Windows

# 2. Install Django
python -m pip install django

# 3. Create project
django-admin startproject django_project .

# 4. Run server
python manage.py runserver

The dot (.) after the project name
keeps files in the current folder.
Without it: nested django_project/django_project/

steps.say: Here is what gets created and what each file does.
add: {b:manage.py} — command runner: runserver, migrate, startapp, shell…
{b:settings.py} — all configuration: installed apps, database, templates, static files
{b:wsgi.py} — interface for traditional servers (Gunicorn, Apache) — {g:used in production}
{b:asgi.py} — interface for async servers (Channels, Uvicorn) — {g:used for WebSockets}
{b:__init__.py} — marks folder as Python package (usually empty)

steps.say: Now create an app inside the project. Apps are reusable modules — one project, many apps.
add:
# settings.py — register the new app
INSTALLED_APPS = [
    'django.contrib.admin',
    'django.contrib.auth',
    # ... built-in apps ...
    'pages',  # ← add your app
]

steps.say: Let's apply the initial migrations before doing anything else. Django's built-in apps need tables in the database.
add:
Always run migrate after creating a project
before running the server.

add.q: What is the correct order when starting a Django project from scratch?
add.ok: startproject → startapp → register in INSTALLED_APPS → migrate → runserver
add.why: You must create the project first, then apps, register them, migrate (create DB tables), then run the server.

boards.title: URL routing — from browser to view

steps.say: URL routing is how Django knows which view to call when a browser visits a URL. It works in two steps: the project delegates to the app.

items: what is left to match: home/

steps.say: Here's the actual code. Notice Django strips the prefix: when pages/urls.py sees the request, the URL is just 'home/', not 'pages/home/'.
add:
# pages/urls.py
from django.urls import path
from .views import home_page_view

urlpatterns = [
    path('home/', home_page_view, name='home'),
]

# django_project/urls.py
from django.contrib import admin
from django.urls import path, include

urlpatterns = [
    path('admin/', admin.site.urls),
    path('pages/', include('pages.urls')),  # string!
]

add.5: ← 'pages.urls' in quotes — common mistake: forgetting quotes

steps.say: URL parameters let you capture values from the URL. The <int:id> part captures an integer and passes it as a keyword argument to the view.
add:
# pages/urls.py
urlpatterns = [
    path('home/', home_page_view, name='home'),
    path('meeting/<int:id>/', detail_view, name='detail'),
]

# views.py
def detail_view(request, id):   # id comes from URL
    meeting = Meeting.objects.get(pk=id)
    return render(request, 'detail.html', {'meeting': meeting})

Type converters: <int:x> integers only
<str:x> any string (default)
<slug:x> letters, digits, hyphens
<uuid:x> UUID format

steps.say: The name= parameter is very powerful: it lets you reverse a URL by name instead of hardcoding the path.
add: # In a template: View meeting # generates: /pages/meeting/5/ # In Python: from django.urls import reverse reverse('detail', args=[5]) # returns '/pages/meeting/5/'
{g:Advantage:} if you change the URL path from 'meeting/<int:id>/' to 'meetings/<int:pk>/', only urls.py changes — {g:all templates and Python code using the name still work}

add.q: You change path('home/', ...) to path('homepage/', ...) but keep name='home'. Does {% url 'home' %} in templates still work?
bad: No — you must update every template manually
No — name= must match the path string
Yes — but only if you restart the server
add.why: Named URLs reverse to whatever path() is currently set to. That's the whole point — the name is stable, the path can change.

steps.say: In the Meeting Planner project we have two apps: 'website' for static pages and 'meetings' for data. Let's trace how a view fetches data and passes it to a template.

add.4: ← context = data to pass to the template

add: {b:render(request, template, context)} = load template + fill in variables + return HttpResponse

steps.say: The context dict maps variable names to values. Inside the template, you use those names with {{ }} and {% %}.
add:
{% extends "base.html" %} {% block content %}

Meetings

    {% for meeting in meetings %}
  • {{ meeting.title }}
    • {% endfor %}
{% endblock %}

add.5: ← 'meetings' comes from the context dict key

steps.say: For the detail view, we need to fetch one specific meeting by ID from the URL. The safe way is get_object_or_404.
add:
# meetings/views.py
from django.shortcuts import get_object_or_404, render
from .models import Meeting

def detail(request, id):
    # SAFE: returns 404 page if not found
    meeting = get_object_or_404(Meeting, id=id)
    return render(request, 'meetings/detail.html', {'meeting': meeting})

add.6: ← UNSAFE version: Meeting.objects.get(pk=id) → 500 crash if missing

add:
.get() → DoesNotExist → 500 server crash {r:✗}
get_object_or_404 → Http404 → 404 page {g:✓}

steps.say: Here's the two-app URL structure for the Meeting Planner — the project urls.py connects both apps.
add:
# meetings_planner/urls.py (project)
from django.contrib import admin
from django.urls import path, include

urlpatterns = [
    path('admin/', admin.site.urls),
    path('website/', include('website.urls')),
    path('meetings/', include('meetings.urls')),
]

# website/urls.py
from django.urls import path
from . import views

urlpatterns = [
    path('', views.home_view, name='home'),
    path('about/', views.about_view, name='about'),
]

add.q: A view calls Meeting.objects.get(pk=999) but no meeting has pk=999. What happens?
add.ok: Meeting.DoesNotExist is raised → Django shows a 500 error page
bad: Django creates a new Meeting with pk=999
add.why: Plain .get() raises DoesNotExist, which is an unhandled exception → 500. Use get_object_or_404 to convert it to a clean 404 response.

steps.say: Template inheritance solves a real problem: every page needs the same DOCTYPE, navigation, CSS, and footer. Without inheritance you copy-paste it into every file — a maintenance nightmare.
The base template defines the shared layout and uses {% block %} as named holes for child templates to fill in.
add:
<!DOCTYPE html>
<html lang="en">
<head>
  <meta charset="UTF-8">
  <title>{% block title %}{% endblock %}</title>
</head>
<body>
  {% block content %}
  {% endblock %}
</body>
</html>

add.4: ← named hole: child fills in the title
add.7: ← named hole: child fills in the page body

steps.say: Child templates use {% extends %} to inherit the base, then fill in the blocks.

add.0: ← MUST be the very first line!

add:
{% extends %} must be LINE 1.
Any content before it is silently discarded.
This is the most common beginner trap.

steps.say: To add CSS, we load the static tag and use {% static %} to generate the correct file URL.
add:
{% load static %}
<!DOCTYPE html>
<html lang="en">
<head>
  <meta charset="UTF-8">
  <title>{% block title %}{% endblock %}</title>
  <link rel="stylesheet"
        href="{% static 'website/style.css' %}">
</head>
<body>
  {% block content %}{% endblock %}
</body>
</html>

add.0: ← must be FIRST LINE when using {% static %}

add.q: A template has {% load static %} on line 3 (after DOCTYPE and <html>). Will {% static 'style.css' %} work?
add.ok: Yes — {% load static %} works anywhere before the first {% static %} use
bad: No — {% load static %} must be line 1 when no extends is used
No — it must be inside {% block %}
Yes only if STATIC_URL is set
add.why: {% load static %} just needs to appear before the first use of {% static %}. When extends is present, {% load static %} must come after {% extends %} (but that's the first line anyway). Without extends, any position before first use is fine.
